direct.title: Pizza Dough Calculator – yeast from time & temperature
direct.description: Free pizza dough calculator: flour, water, salt and yeast in grams, with the yeast worked out from your fermentation time and temperature. Neapolitan, New York and Roman presets, cold fermentation, metric and imperial.
direct.heading: Pizza Dough Calculator
direct.guideTitle: How the pizza dough calculator works
direct.intro: Most dough recipes fix the amount of yeast and leave you to fit your day around it. This calculator works the other way round: you say how long the dough has and how warm it will be, and it works out the yeast that makes the dough ready on time. Everything else follows from the number of pizzas, the weight of each dough ball and the dough's baker's percentages.

poolish.title: Poolish Pizza Dough Calculator – poolish yeast by time
poolish.description: Calculate poolish pizza dough: flour, water and yeast for the poolish and the final dough in grams, with the yeast worked out from how long and how warm the poolish ripens. Free, metric and imperial.
poolish.heading: Poolish Pizza Calculator
poolish.intro: A poolish is a preferment of equal parts flour and water with a pinch of yeast, left to ripen for several hours before the dough is mixed. This calculator splits the recipe into the poolish and the final dough, sets the poolish yeast so it peaks when you need it, and adds only as much yeast to the final dough as its own schedule still needs.

sections.heading: What a poolish does
paragraphs: During its long, wet ripening the poolish builds aroma and enzymes that gently break down starch and gluten. The result is a dough that stretches easily, a light, open crust and a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavour — without the sourness of a sourdough.
For pizza, 25–35 % of the flour in the poolish is typical. More gives a stronger flavour and a more extensible dough, and the final dough then needs less yeast, or none at all.

sections.heading: When the poolish is ripe
paragraphs: A ripe poolish has doubled or tripled, is full of bubbles and smells fruity and slightly sweet. Use it when the dome is just starting to flatten. Once it has collapsed and smells sharply sour or of alcohol, it has gone too far.

The amount of yeast decides when that point comes: the longer and cooler, the less yeast. A 16-hour poolish needs only a fraction of the yeast of a 4-hour one. If your plans change, a ripe poolish keeps in the fridge for up to about a day.

faq.question: How much poolish should pizza dough have?
faq.answer: Usually 25–35 % of the total flour; this calculator starts at 30 %. Up to 50 % gives a stronger flavour and an even more extensible dough.

faq.question: Does poolish pizza dough need extra yeast?
faq.answer: Often only a little. The ripe poolish already brings plenty of active yeast, so the calculator adds only what the final dough's own schedule still needs — and none at all if the poolish alone is enough.

faq.question: Can a poolish go in the fridge?
faq.answer: A poolish ripens best in the warmth, so let it ripen at room temperature first. A ripe poolish then keeps in the fridge for up to about 24 hours; let it warm up for 30–60 minutes before mixing it into the dough.

direct.label: Direct (yeast only)
direct.hint: All the yeast goes into one dough. The simplest method — the flavour comes from the fermentation schedule alone.

poolish.label: Poolish
poolish.hint: Part of the flour ferments for several hours first, as a runny preferment of equal flour and water. Gives a more extensible dough, a lighter crust and a mild, slightly sweet aroma.
poolish.shareTooltip: How much of the recipe's total flour goes into the poolish. 25–35 % is typical for pizza; up to 50 % for more flavour and a very extensible dough.
poolish.hydrationTooltip: Water in the poolish, as a percentage of its own flour.
poolish.timeTooltip: Hours until the poolish is ripe. The yeast is set so it peaks just then: the longer and cooler, the less yeast.
poolish.yeastNote: Poolish yeast: {{percent}} % {{yeast}} relative to the poolish flour.
poolish.noExtraYeast: No extra yeast in the final dough — the ripe poolish leavens it on its own.
poolish.surplus: The poolish alone brings more leavening than this schedule needs, so no yeast goes into the final dough — and the dough will still be ready early, after about {{hours}} h at room temperature instead of {{planned}} h. Shorten the room-temperature time or use less poolish.
poolish.surplusTooShort: The poolish alone brings more leavening than even the shortest schedule needs, so the dough will be ready early. Use less poolish or add a longer cold phase.
poolish.step: Poolish, {{hours}} h before you mix the dough: stir {{flour}} flour, {{water}} water and {{yeast}} yeast into a smooth batter. Cover and leave at {{temp}} until it has doubled or tripled, is full of bubbles and the dome is just starting to settle.
poolish.knead: Mix the dough: loosen the poolish in the water and the ice, add the flour{{yeast}} and mix until no dry flour is left, then work in the salt. Knead for 10–15 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.

pizzaStyleHints.neapolitan: 65 % hydration, small soft dough balls, short bake at very high heat.
pizzaStyleHints.newyork: Slightly drier dough with oil and sugar, long cold fermentation, crisp base.
pizzaStyleHints.roman: Very wet dough for thin, crunchy pizza — usually baked in a tray or on a stone.
pizzaStyleHints.custom: Neutral starting point — change every value to your own recipe.

calculator.doughBallWeightTooltip: Weight of the dough for a single pizza.
calculator.waterPercentTooltip: Hydration as a percentage of the flour weight.
calculator.icePercentTooltip: How much of the water to weigh out as ice — a percentage of the water, not of the flour. The ice is not extra liquid: it melts in, so the hydration is unchanged. Melting absorbs heat, which keeps the dough cool through a long knead. Around 10 % suits hand kneading; go higher for a mixer or a warm kitchen, or 0 to skip it.
calculator.saltPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight. 2–3 % is typical.
calculator.autoCalculateYeast: Calculate yeast automatically from time and temperature

fermentation.roomTimeTooltip: Total time at room temperature, split over the bulk rise and the final proof. At least {{minimum}} h are needed.
fermentation.coldTimeTooltip: Time in the fridge between the bulk rise and balling. Set 0 to skip the cold fermentation.

split.label: Split of the room-temperature time
split.tooltip: Where the room-temperature hours go: rising as one piece before the fridge, or proving as balls after it. Longer bulk builds flavour and gluten; longer final proof gives lighter balls that are easier to stretch.
split.noSlack: Raise the room-temperature time above {{minimum}} h to shift hours between the two phases.

fresh.label: Fresh yeast (cake yeast)
fresh.hint: The moist block from the fridge. Crumble it straight into the dough or dissolve it in part of the water. This is the reference amount all other types are converted from.

instant.label: Instant dry yeast
instant.hint: Fine granules that are stirred straight into the flour — no soaking needed. You need about 40 % of the fresh-yeast amount.

active.label: Active dry yeast (needs rehydrating)
active.hint: Coarser granules that must first be woken up: stir into lukewarm water (about {{temp}}) with a pinch of sugar and wait 10 minutes until it foams, then add it to the dough. You need about 50 % of the fresh-yeast amount.

calculator.yeastPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight, for the yeast type selected above.
calculator.yeastPercentFinalTooltip: Yeast added to the final dough, as a percentage of the total flour. At 0 the preferment does all the leavening.
calculator.oilPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight (0 = no oil). Makes the base softer and browner.
calculator.sugarPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight (0 = no sugar). Helps the crust colour in a home oven.

afterCold.label: After the cold fermentation
afterCold.hint: The whole batch goes into the fridge as one mass and is divided when it comes out. The mass cools slowly, so it keeps fermenting for hours on the way down — less yeast is needed.

beforeCold.label: Before the cold fermentation
beforeCold.hint: The dough is divided and balled before it goes into the fridge. Balls chill much faster than a single mass, so they bank less fermentation while cooling — slightly more yeast is needed. Easier to store, and the balls are ready to use straight from the fridge.

thermalModel.label: Account for the dough cooling down
thermalModel.onHint: The fridge phase is weighted by how long the dough actually takes to get cold, which depends on the batch size and on whether it is retarded in bulk or as balls.
thermalModel.offHint: The original estimate: the fridge phase counts as plain wall-clock hours, whatever the size or shape of the dough.

sections.heading: Baker's percentages
paragraphs: Every ingredient is given as a percentage of the flour weight, with the flour itself at 100 %. A Neapolitan dough at 65 % hydration and 2.5 % salt uses 650 g of water and 25 g of salt for each kilogram of flour.

To get from there to grams, the calculator adds up all the percentages and divides the total dough weight — pizzas × ball weight — by that sum. That gives the flour, and every other ingredient is the flour times its percentage.

sections.heading: Yeast from time and temperature
paragraphs: Yeast works faster the warmer it is and the longer it has, so the same dough can need ten times more yeast for a same-day bake than for a three-day cold ferment. The calculator models the room-temperature hours and the fridge hours separately and combines them, so any mix of the two gives a sensible amount.
Fresh, instant and active dry yeast are converted automatically: instant dry yeast is about 40 % of the fresh-yeast weight, active dry yeast about 50 %.

sections.heading: Cold fermentation in the fridge
paragraphs: A long, cold rest builds flavour and makes the dough easier to stretch, without it over-proving. The fridge does not stop fermentation though: the dough takes hours to cool down, and it keeps working while it does.

How long depends on its size. A whole batch retarded in one piece cools much more slowly than the same dough divided into balls, so it banks more fermentation on the way down and needs a little less yeast. The calculator accounts for this when it is switched on.

items.question: How long should pizza dough ferment?
items.answer: A same-day dough needs at least 5 hours at room temperature. Most pizzerias ferment for 24 to 72 hours with most of that time in the fridge, which gives more flavour and a dough that is easier to stretch. Choose the schedule that fits your day, and the calculator sets the yeast to match.

items.question: What hydration should pizza dough have?
items.answer: Neapolitan dough is usually around 60–65 % water, New York style around 60–63 % with a little oil and sugar, and Roman-style pizza 70–80 %. Higher hydration gives a lighter, more open crust but is stickier to handle.

items.question: How do I convert fresh yeast to dry yeast?
items.answer: Use about 40 % of the fresh-yeast weight for instant dry yeast and about 50 % for active dry yeast. 10 g of fresh yeast becomes about 4 g instant or 5 g active dry. Pick the yeast type in the calculator and it converts for you.

items.question: Should the dough go into the fridge in one piece or as balls?
items.answer: Both work. In one piece the dough cools slowly and keeps fermenting for hours on the way down, so it needs slightly less yeast and is shaped after the fridge. As balls it chills faster, needs slightly more yeast, and can go straight from the fridge to the final proof.

items.question: Why add ice to pizza dough?
items.answer: Kneading warms the dough, and warm dough ferments faster than planned. Weighing part of the water as ice keeps it cool. The ice is not extra water — the hydration stays the same — and about 10 % of the water is enough for hand kneading.

footer.privacy: No cookies, no tracking, no analytics, and no external fonts or scripts. The calculator runs entirely in your browser — nothing you enter is ever sent to a server. The only thing kept is your chosen language and unit system, saved in this browser so the page remembers them; clearing your site data removes them again.
